summary: Depth-first rabbithole dossier for $merge and $out Materialized Views; source-anchored research pack.

facts.text: 9. "Atomic" here means all-or-nothing, not non-blocking. The final `renameCollection` takes exclusive locks: on a sharded cluster "the source and target collections are exclusively locked on every shard," and "subsequent operations on the source and target collections must wait until the `renameCollection` completes." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/renameCollection/>

**Concept:** `$merge` and `$out` Materialized Views **Parent domain:** MongoDB Aggregation Pipeline **Report type:** mechanism (internal workings, parts, invariants, limits) **Researched:** 2026-09-18 **Manual version observed:** MongoDB Database Manual, current channel (renders as 8.3)

This report covers only the two terminal aggregation stages that persist pipeline output to a collection — `$merge` and `$out` — and the "on-demand materialized view" pattern MongoDB builds on top of them. In scope: stage syntax and its parts, the write mechanism each stage uses, the invariants each does and does not guarantee (atomicity, index requirements, matching semantics), and documented limits.

37. The cross-database `into: { db, coll }` capability was tracked as SERVER-13201, "Allow new Aggregation `$merge` stage to explicitly name a DB to write to," created 2014-03-14, resolved 2018-08-28, fix version 4.1.3 — the development series preceding 4.2. The ticket was originally filed against `$out`'s inability to name a database and was retitled once `$merge` became the vehicle; it contains no design discussion of incremental refresh. <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13201>

**C2. `$out` funnels the merger stage through the primary shard.** The pipeline's merger part "executes this *merger part* on the designated primary shard, which holds the referenced unsharded collection" — a single-node write bottleneck and a hotspot on the primary shard for large snapshot rebuilds. <https://www.practical-mongodb-aggregations.com/guides/sharding.html>

**C3. On a sharded cluster, `$merge`'s output database must pre-exist, and `on` must contain every shard key field.** "For a sharded cluster, the specified output database must already exist." If the target is sharded, `on` "defaults to all the shard key fields and the `_id` field. If specifying a different `on` identifier, the `on` must contain all the shard key fields." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

66 numbered claims (S1–S66) in 8 parts, 10 disagreements (D1–D10), 7 gaps (G1–G7), a per-dimension saturation verdict, and 39 deduped sources across 14 hosts. Every claim tagged with which of the four reports support it.

4. As shipped, `$out` could only overwrite. The same 2014 source states: "`$out` doesn't have any way of appending to the output collection, it can only overwrite the output collection." https://thecodebarbarian.com/2014/04/25/a-nodejs-perspective-on-whats-new-in-mongodb-2-6-part-ii-aggregation-out.html

15. The contrast with standard views is storage, not semantics: "Standard views are computed when you read the view, and are not stored to disk. On-demand materialized views are stored on and read from disk. They use a `$merge` or `$out` stage to update the saved data." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/

1. MongoDB Manual — On-Demand Materialized Views: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/ 2. MongoDB Manual — `$merge` (aggregation stage): https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/ 3. MongoDB Manual — `$out` (aggregation stage): https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/ 4. MongoDB Manual — Change Streams: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/changeStreams/ 5. MongoDB Manual — `renameCollection`: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/renameCollection/ 6. MongoDB Blog (2025-09-09) — Real-Time Mater

Out of scope, and deliberately not researched: standard (non-materialized) MongoDB views, Atlas Stream Processing as a product, Atlas Scheduled Triggers, time series collections as a feature, and the general database theory of incremental view maintenance beyond the one origin claim needed to date the term.

9. Cross-database output for the new stage was tracked in SERVER-13201, created 2014-03-14 and retitled "Allow new Aggregation $merge stage to explicitly name a DB to write to", resolved with fix version 4.1.3. The original 2014 request was about `$out` and was motivated by write-lock contention when parallel aggregations all wrote into the same database. https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13201

Out of scope and deliberately not researched: standard (non-materialized) views, Atlas Stream Processing, change streams as a refresh driver, other aggregation stages, scheduling/trigger infrastructure, and the surrounding aggregation framework. Those are separate frontier items.

26. From MongoDB 5.0, pipelines containing `$merge` may run on replica set secondaries when cluster-wide `featureCompatibilityVersion` is 5.0 or higher and read preference allows secondary reads; `$merge` and `$out` execute on the secondary but their write operations are routed to the primary. Driver support for this is not universal. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

34. Deletion in the source has no mechanism in either stage. A `$merge` refresh only inserts and matches; it never removes a target document whose source rows have disappeared. `$out`'s full replacement is the only one of the two that implicitly drops vanished rows. MongoDB positions Atlas Stream Processing, not `$merge`, as the facility that "can delete documents from the target collection when a corresponding deletion event is detected." <https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/technical/real-time-materialized-views-with-atlas-stream-processing>

15. Refresh is not automatic. Teams drive it on demand, on a schedule (cron or Atlas Scheduled Triggers running the `$out`/`$merge` pipeline periodically), or incrementally from change streams; the third is "more complex to set up and manage." ([Mayallo, dev.to, 2025-05-13](https://dev.to/mayallo/mongodb-views-or-materialized-views-when-to-use-46d8))

**E3. Historical precedent that `$out` output is not inherently durable.** SERVER-23274: in MongoDB 3.2 (3.1.9 through 3.2.x before the fix), `$out`-created collections were incorrectly flagged temporary and were dropped during replica set elections, causing silent data loss; fixed in 3.2.5 / 3.3.4. Not a live defect, but evidence that the atomic-rename mechanism has a history of interacting badly with replication events — worth weighing before treating a `$out` view as a system of record. <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-23274>

28. When `$out` writes to an existing time series collection, the existing collection must already be a time series collection, must not be a view, and the `timeseries` options in the `$out` stage must exactly match those on the existing collection. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

**C. Whether the database "maintains" the view.** The 2019-07-16 Percona Community post says that with `$merge` "the database will take the responsibility to build and maintain the view" (https://percona.community/blog/2019/07/16/concept-materialized-views-mongodb-sharded-clusters/). MongoDB's own documentation does not support the "maintain" half: refresh happens only when a caller re-runs the pipeline (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/), and the Atlas comparison labels on-demand refresh as "Manual or scheduled" (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-proce

10. The rename is cheap only because source and destination share a database: "If the target database is the same as the source database, `renameCollection` simply changes the namespace. This is a quick operation." A cross-database `$out` copies all documents and its duration depends on collection size. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/renameCollection/>

19. `$merge` has an insertion shortcut: when `whenMatched` is a pipeline, `whenNotMatched` is `insert`, and no match exists, the document is inserted directly without executing the pipeline. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

24. Evaluation is a freshness/cost trade, stated by a third-party practitioner as "Materialized Views = Fast Reads (but Complexity + Stale Data + Storage Costs)." The view duplicates data, so storage cost is an explicit axis alongside latency. ([Mayallo, dev.to, 2025-05-13](https://dev.to/mayallo/mongodb-views-or-materialized-views-when-to-use-46d8))

**B1. `$merge` writing into the collection it reads can loop forever (Halloween Problem).** "When `$merge` outputs to the same collection that is being aggregated, documents may get updated multiple times or the operation may result in an infinite loop. This behavior occurs when the update performed by `$merge` changes the physical location of documents stored on disk." The manual names the classic cause explicitly. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> · <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween_Problem>

**D3. `$out` concurrent with a `mongodump --oplog` fails the backup.** "A `mongodump` started with `--oplog` fails if a client issues an aggregation pipeline that includes `$out` during the dump process." A scheduled view refresh can break an unrelated backup window. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

22. `$merge` may output to the same collection being aggregated, but doing so is hazardous: "documents may get updated multiple times or the operation may result in an infinite loop. This behavior occurs when the update performed by `$merge` changes the physical location of documents stored on disk. When the physical location of a document changes, `$merge` may view it as an entirely new document, resulting in additional updates." MongoDB names this the Halloween Problem. No guard is documented; avoidance is the user's responsibility. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/agg

4. **`$merge` version attribution is secondary-sourced.** Claim 36 rests on Severalnines. The `/docs/v4.2/` manual URLs redirect to the current manual, so I could not read the 4.2-era primary page. The SERVER-13201 fix version 4.1.3 (<https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13201>) is consistent with a 4.2 GA but does not itself establish when the stage shipped.

6. SERVER-13201 — Allow new Aggregation `$merge` stage to explicitly name a DB to write to. Created 2014-03-14, resolved 2018-08-28, fix version 4.1.3. <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13201> 7. SERVER-68845 — BSONObjectTooLarge when `$merge` during aggregation. Created 2022-08-08, closed 2022-10-04 (duplicate of SERVER-66289). <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-68845>

13. `$merge` requires a unique index whose keys correspond to the `on` identifier fields. The index must be created before the pipeline runs when `on` is anything other than the default. ([$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))

18. `$merge` may write to the same collection it aggregates, but when it does, "documents may get updated multiple times or the operation may result in an infinite loop" — the manual names this the Halloween Problem. ([$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/), [Halloween Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween_Problem))
Run date: 2026-09-18 Parent concept: MongoDB Aggregation Pipeline Concept under study: `$merge` and `$out` Materialized Views

**E1. `$merge` is not a performance-neutral substitute for `$out` — a reported ~160× gap, closed "Works as Designed."** SERVER-70106 reports, on MongoDB 6.0.1: `insert_many` of 10k records 748 ms; `$densify` + `$out` 565 ms; the same pipeline with `$merge` 91,983 ms. The ticket was closed **Works as Designed** with no optimization guidance; the reporter noted that setting `_id` in the pipeline before `$merge` improved performance. This disconfirms the common "use `$merge` for everything, it is the modern `$out`" guidance for bulk rebuilds. <https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-70106>

**U2. Why `$merge` is ~160× slower than `$out` in SERVER-70106 is undocumented.** The prevailing explanation — that `$merge` performs a document-by-document upsert while `$out` does a bulk insert plus rename — appears only in secondary sources, not in the ticket or the manual. MongoDB closed the ticket without a technical rationale. The magnitude is also unreplicated: one reporter, one pipeline (`$densify`), one version (6.0.1), 2022-era. Do not generalize the ratio without benchmarking your own pipeline.

4. **Cost of a `$merge` refresh at scale.** No source located here quantifies `$merge`'s per-document upsert cost against `$out`'s bulk-insert-plus-rename, or the write-contention impact of a large `$merge` on a live cluster. The practitioner-level claims about "10x gains" and "schedule during off-peak hours" surfaced in search summaries were not verified against a primary, dated benchmark and are therefore excluded from the claims above.

**Concept:** `$merge` and `$out` Materialized Views **Parent domain:** MongoDB Aggregation Pipeline **Report type:** boundary conditions, failure modes, disagreements, disconfirming evidence **Date:** 2026-09-18

This report covers only the two aggregation write stages used to build MongoDB on-demand materialized views — `$out` (full snapshot replace) and `$merge` (incremental upsert) — and the durability, atomicity, concurrency, sharding, and error-reporting boundaries of that pattern. It does **not** cover sibling concepts (standard non-materialized views, Atlas Stream Processing materialized views, `$lookup`, change-stream-driven denormalization) except where an official source draws a direct boundary against them.

**C4. `$out` cannot write to capped collections; `$merge` cannot write to time series collections — and `$out` can.** "The `$out` operator cannot write results to a capped collection." Conversely, "An aggregation pipeline cannot use `$merge` to output to a time series collection," while `$out` supports time series targets provided the existing collection is a time series collection, is not a view, and its `timeseries` options "exactly match those on the existing collection." Time-series materialized views are therefore `$out`-only, which forfeits incremental refresh. <https://www.mongodb.com/d

**C1. `$out` cannot target a sharded collection; `$merge` can.** "You cannot specify a sharded collection as the output collection... To output to a sharded collection, see `$merge`." This is the hard fork in the design space: a materialized view larger than one shard's capacity cannot use `$out`. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

**C5. Both stages are barred from view definitions and from nested pipelines.** Neither `$out` nor `$merge` is allowed "as part of a view definition," and both are forbidden inside the nested pipelines of `$lookup`, `$facet`, and `$unionWith` — the restriction propagates into nested pipelines of a view definition too. A materialized view cannot be defined declaratively; it must be driven by an external scheduler. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/> · <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

**D1. `$out` breaks change streams on the view; `$merge` does not.** "When using `$merge`, you can use change streams to watch for changes on the materialized view. When using `$out`, you can't watch for changes on the materialized view." The mechanism is A1: the rename/drop raises an `invalidate` event, and "You cannot use `resumeAfter` to resume a change stream after an invalidate event (for example, a collection drop or rename) closes the stream." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/> · <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/change-events/invalidate/>

**A5. Neither stage can be wrapped in a transaction to recover atomicity.** "An aggregation pipeline cannot use `$merge` inside a transaction." / "An aggregation pipeline cannot use `$out` inside transactions." So the A3 partial-write window cannot be closed by the obvious mitigation. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> · <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

**A4. Schema validation splits a `$merge` batch; it does not split an `$out`.** With `validationAction: error`, `$merge` writes every valid document and fails only the invalid ones, and "If there are multiple invalid documents, only the first invalid document encountered throws an error." The same condition under `$out` "makes no changes to the pre-existing collection." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> · <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

**A6. Neither stage is retryable by the driver.** The MongoDB driver specification lists, under unsupported write operations: "Write commands other than insert, update, delete, or findAndModify are not supported. This includes, but is not limited to, an aggregate command using a write stage (e.g. `$out`, `$merge`)." Drivers "MUST NOT add a transaction ID to these commands and MUST NOT retry these commands if they fail to return a response." A view refresh that loses its connection mid-flight is therefore neither rolled back (A3) nor retried. <https://github.com/mongodb/specifications/blob/mast

**B5. MongoDB 8.3 adds a collation check that can refuse a previously-working pipeline.** "Starting in MongoDB 8.3, the server checks to ensure that the automatically created `_id` index matches the query's collation. If the collations do not match, the `_id` index cannot provide uniqueness for the query, and the query will not run." This is a forward-compatibility break for collation-using views. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

**B7. `$merge` never deletes. Incremental views accumulate tombstoneless staleness.** `$merge`'s behavior space is `whenMatched: replace|keepExisting|merge|fail|pipeline` and `whenNotMatched: insert|discard|fail` — there is no delete disposition, so documents whose source rows disappeared persist in the view until the operator removes them explicitly. Third-party guidance treats explicit pre-merge deletion of the refreshed range as the required pattern. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> · <https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-merge-increm

**C6. Neither stage is compatible with `"linearizable"` read concern.** "if you specify `"linearizable"` read concern for `db.collection.aggregate()`, you cannot include the `$merge` stage in the pipeline" — and the same sentence appears for `$out`. A view refresh cannot be given the strongest read guarantee. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> · <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

**E4. Widely-cited secondary write-ups omit precisely the failure modes above.** A dated third-party comparison (2026-03-31) states that `$out` "drops the collection and creates a new one atomically" and that `$out` "cannot write to a sharded collection," but does not address reader visibility during the swap, `$merge` partial-write risk, or any performance comparison. Practitioners relying on such summaries will not learn about A3, E1, or E2. <https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-difference-between-merge-and-out-in-mongodb/view>

1. The term "materialized view" and the problem of keeping one current against changing base data were established in the database literature well before MongoDB. The canonical survey is A. Gupta and I. S. Mumick, "Maintenance of Materialized Views: Problems, Techniques, and Applications", *IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin* 18(2), pp. 3–18, 1995. Bibliographic record: https://pubs.dbs.uni-leipzig.de/se/node/395 *Confidence caveat: this citation was verified from a bibliographic index record and from search metadata, not from a fetched full text. Treat the volume/page numbers as secondary.*

17. The two stages differ in what you can observe afterwards: "When using `$merge`, you can use change streams to watch for changes on the materialized view. When using `$out`, you can't watch for changes on the materialized view." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/

27. Time series is the reverse asymmetry, and it is newer: "Starting in MongoDB 7.0.3 and 7.1, `$out` can take a document to output to a time series collection", while `$merge` "Cannot output to a time series collection." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

33. `$out` cannot write to a capped collection, and if it modifies a collection carrying a MongoDB Search index you must delete and re-create that search index — the docs recommend `$merge` instead in that case. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

**A. MongoDB's own docs contradict each other on when `$merge` gained cross-database output.** The 4.2 release notes list "Can output to a collection in the same or different database" as a capability of the new 4.2 stage (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/release-notes/4.2.md), and SERVER-13201 — the cross-database ticket for the new `$merge` stage — carries fix version 4.1.3, inside the 4.2 development series (https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-13201). But the 4.4 release notes state: "`$merge` can output to a collection in a different database. In earlier versions, `$merge` can only out

28. `$out` cannot write to a capped collection. `$merge` cannot write to a time series collection; `$out` can, via the `timeseries` form, subject to the existing collection being a time series collection, not a view, and having `timeseries` options that "exactly match" those in the `$out` stage. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/> <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

5. `$out` cannot write to a sharded output collection; the input collection may be sharded. `$merge` can write to a sharded collection and read from a sharded input. On a sharded target, the `on` identifier must include all shard key fields. ([$out reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/), [$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))

6. The capability runs the other way for time series: `$out` can write to a time series collection (syntax added in MongoDB 7.0.3 and 7.1), while "an aggregation pipeline cannot use `$merge` to output to a time series collection." ([$out reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/), [$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))

- **Pick `$out` for a full nightly rebuild of an unsharded, non-search-indexed reporting collection.** You get atomic reader-visible swap (claim 8) and automatic index re-creation, at the cost of recomputing everything and losing change-stream observability (claim 7). - **Pick `$merge` for anything incremental, sharded, or watched.** Accept that a failed refresh leaves the view half-updated (claim 9), so the pipeline must be idempotent and safe to re-run for a given key range (claim 12). - **Design the `on` key first.** It determines the required unique index (claim 13), the sharding constrain

**A3. A failed `$merge` leaves partial writes behind — this is the single largest operational hazard of the incremental pattern.** "If the aggregation fails, any writes completed by the `$merge` before the error will not be rolled back." The manual repeats this for `_id`/shard-key modification errors as well. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

**B3. `$merge` requires a pre-existing unique index that is not partial and matches the aggregation collation.** "`$merge` requires a unique index with keys that correspond to the `on` identifier fields... the unique index must only contain the `on` fields as its keys." It "can be a sparse index" but "cannot be a partial index," and "must also have the same collation as the aggregation's collation." "For output collections that already exist, the corresponding index must already exist." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

**B4. Null/missing `on` values are a version boundary.** "For deployments running MongoDB 8.0 and earlier, specified field or fields for `on` cannot be missing or contain a null value. Starting in MongoDB 8.1, if the supporting index is not sparse, the specified field or fields for `on` can be missing or contain a null value." Arrays remain forbidden in all versions. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

**B8. The `whenMatched` pipeline is a restricted sub-language.** Only `$addFields`/`$set`, `$project`/`$unset`, and `$replaceRoot`/`$replaceWith` are permitted, and "The pipeline cannot modify the `on` field's value." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

3. `$out` shipped to users in MongoDB 2.6 (April 2014). A contemporaneous account dated 2014-04-25 records that 2.6 "introduced a `$out` aggregation pipeline stage, which writes the output of the aggregation to a separate collection, and removed the 16MB aggregation limit", and that before 2.6 "aggregation results were limited to 16MB in size". https://thecodebarbarian.com/2014/04/25/a-nodejs-perspective-on-whats-new-in-mongodb-2-6-part-ii-aggregation-out.html

18. You can index an on-demand materialized view directly, which you cannot do with a standard view: "You can also create indexes directly on on-demand materialized views because MongoDB stores those indexes on disk." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/

20. `$merge` defaults are `whenMatched: "merge"` and `whenNotMatched: "insert"`; the full option sets are `replace | keepExisting | merge | fail | <pipeline>` and `insert | discard | fail`. A custom `whenMatched` pipeline may use only `$addFields`, `$project`, and `$replaceRoot`. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/

23. Self-targeted `$merge` carries an explicit correctness warning: "When `$merge` outputs to the same collection that is being aggregated, documents may get updated multiple times or the operation may result in an infinite loop. This behavior occurs when the update performed by `$merge` changes the physical location of documents stored on disk." MongoDB names this the Halloween Problem and links to https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Halloween_Problem&oldid=738886300 Warning text: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/release-notes/4.4.md

26. Sharding is the durable asymmetry between the stages: `$out` "Cannot output to a sharded collection. Input collection, however, can be sharded", whereas `$merge` "Can output to a sharded collection. Input collection can also be sharded." This has held from 4.2 through the current manual. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

29. MongoDB 8.1 relaxed the `on` field constraint for `$merge`: "For deployments running MongoDB 8.0 and earlier, specified field or fields for `on` cannot be missing or contain a null value. Starting in MongoDB 8.1, if the supporting index is not sparse, the specified field or fields for `on` can be missing or contain a null value." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/

30. MongoDB 8.3 added a collation check: "Starting in MongoDB 8.3, the server checks to ensure that the automatically created `_id` index matches the query's collation. If the collations do not match, the `_id` index cannot provide uniqueness for the query, and the query will not run." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/

8. `$out` is fail-safe with respect to the old contents: "If the aggregation fails, the `$out` operation makes no changes to the pre-existing collection." The same holds for schema-validation failures when `validationAction` is `error` — no changes are made and no pipeline documents are added. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

15. `on` field values may not be arrays, and must be present in the pipeline results (except `_id`, which is generated if absent). Through MongoDB 8.0 the `on` fields "cannot be missing or contain a null value"; starting in MongoDB 8.1 they may be null or missing if the supporting index is not sparse. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

16. `whenMatched` (default `"merge"`) selects one of five behaviours on a match: `replace`, `keepExisting`, `merge` (field-level union, in the manner of `$mergeObjects`), `fail`, or a custom aggregation pipeline restricted to `$addFields`/`$set`, `$project`/`$unset`, and `$replaceRoot`/`$replaceWith`. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

20. `$merge` is not all-or-nothing. On a `fail` action, "any changes to the output collection from previous documents are not reverted." Under schema validation with `validationAction: error`, "all valid documents are written to the target collection, and all invalid documents fail to write" — a partial write by design. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

27. Sharded output is the sharpest capability split: `$merge` can write to a sharded output collection; `$out` cannot — "You cannot specify a sharded collection as the output collection." Read operations of the `$out` statement occur on the secondary nodes, while the write operations occur only on the primary nodes." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

2. The `$out` stage originates in MongoDB server ticket SERVER-3253, "aggregation: unsharded support $out", created 2011-06-13 and resolved 2013-08-08 with fix version 2.5.2 (a development release in the series that became 2.6). https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-3253

7. That `$out`-modes design was then superseded by a separate stage. SERVER-40429, "Add $merge stage to write output to existing collection", was created 2019-04-01, resolved 2019-05-02, fix version 4.1.11. Its description states plainly: "This stage replaces the new modes of $out." https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-40429

21. MongoDB 4.4 allowed `$merge` to write back into the collection being aggregated: "Starting in MongoDB 4.4, `$merge` can output to the same collection that is being aggregated. You can also output to a collection which appears in other stages of the pipeline, such as `$lookup`." and "Versions of MongoDB prior to 4.4 did not allow `$merge` to output to the same collection as the collection being aggregated." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/release-notes/4.4.md

MongoDB 4.4 allowed the read side of both stages to run on secondaries, gated on `featureCompatibilityVersion` 4.4 and a read preference allowing secondary reads; the write side still runs only on the primary. The current manual restates the same gate at FCV 5.0. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/release-notes/4.4.md and https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

36. The comparison page classifies the on-demand view as running "manually or on a schedule", with latency "minutes to days", freshness "point-in-time snapshot", and compute model "Recomputes full result"; the streaming view is "change-driven, continuous", sub-second, "perpetually synchronized", and "Computes incremental effect". The two are described as complementary: initialize with a `$merge` batch aggregation, then start a stream processor over the same collection. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-stream-processing/streaming-materialized-views/

5. `$out` takes three syntactic forms: a bare collection string (`{ $out: "<coll>" }`), a document naming a database and collection (`{ $out: { db: ..., coll: ... } }`), and — from MongoDB 7.0.3 — a form carrying `timeseries` options (`timeField`, `metaField`, `granularity`). <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

6. `$out` replaces an existing target through a four-step swap: it (1) creates a temp collection, (2) copies the index definitions from the existing collection to the temp collection, (3) inserts the documents into the temp collection, and (4) calls `renameCollection` with `dropTarget: true` to rename the temp collection to the destination. The docs describe the net effect as: `$out` "atomically replaces it upon completion of the aggregation." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

12. `$merge` accepts five fields: `into` (required), and optional `on`, `let`, `whenMatched`, and `whenNotMatched`. `into` may be a collection string or a `{ db, coll }` document. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

13. `on` names the field or fields that act as the unique identifier used to match a pipeline result document against a document already in the target. Its default depends on the target: `_id` for a non-existent or existing unsharded collection, and all shard key fields plus `_id` for an existing sharded collection. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

14. A unique index whose keys correspond to the `on` fields must already exist on the target. The index must use the same collation as the aggregation, may be sparse, and may not be a partial index. This is the load-bearing invariant of `$merge`: matching is index-enforced, not scan-based. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

23. Both stages must be the last stage in the pipeline. `$merge`: "must be the *last* stage in the pipeline." `$out`: "must be *the last stage* in the pipeline." <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

24. Neither stage may be used inside a transaction, in a view definition, or in the nested pipeline of `$lookup`, `$facet`, or `$unionWith`. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/> <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>

25. Neither stage may be combined with read concern `"linearizable"`. `$out` is explicitly permitted with read concern `"majority"`. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/> <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/>

32. The documented refresh pattern is a parameterised, re-runnable pipeline: a leading `$match` bounds the source range, a `$group` computes the aggregate, and `$merge` with `whenMatched: "replace"` writes it — so re-running with a later bound updates the touched buckets and inserts new ones without reprocessing history. <https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/>

1. **Is `$out`'s "atomic" replacement actually invisible to readers?** The `$out` reference asserts the stage "atomically replaces" the target (<https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/>), while the `renameCollection` reference says both collections are exclusively locked and "subsequent operations … must wait" (<https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/renameCollection/>). Read together, "atomic" means readers never see a half-written collection, but they can block. On a replica set from MongoDB 8.3.12, cross-database renames are documented as permi

4. `$out` replaces the whole target collection; `$merge` incorporates results into an existing collection by inserting, merging, replacing, keeping, failing, or running a custom update pipeline per document. `$merge` is therefore the incremental-refresh stage. ([$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))

10. The documented incremental pattern is a `$match` prefix that restricts the pipeline to the changed slice, followed by `$merge` with `whenMatched: "replace"`. The manual's example filters `year: { $gte: startYear }` before `$group` and `$merge` into `movieYearStats`, so a caller can refresh only 2016-onward rows. ([MongoDB Manual](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/))

14. The default `on` is `_id` for a non-existent or unsharded target, and all shard key fields plus `_id` for a sharded target. ([$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))

21. `$out` destroys and recreates the target collection, so "if the `$out` operation modifies a collection with a MongoDB Search index, you must delete and re-create the search index." A search-indexed view is a poor fit for `$out`. ([$out reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/))

5. The replace is implemented as a rename, not an in-place mutation. MongoDB documents the sequence: `$out` creates a temp collection, copies the index definitions from the existing collection, inserts the documents, then calls `renameCollection` with `dropTarget: true`. If the aggregation fails, `$out` makes no changes to the pre-existing collection. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

8. The `whenMatched: "merge"` behaviour — the field-level merge that distinguishes `$merge` from a plain upsert — was added separately in SERVER-40430, also fix version 4.1.11. https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-40430

16. Refresh is caller-driven. The documented example defines an `updateMovieStats(startYear)` function and says: "To refresh `movieYearStats` for 2016 onward, run the function with a `startYear` of `2016`." Nothing in the server refreshes the view on its own. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/

That capability was implemented in SERVER-42137, "Allow aggregation $merge stage to write to a collection that the query also reads from", created 2019-07-10, resolved 2019-11-20, fix version 4.3.2 (a development release in the series that became 4.4). https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-42137

24. MongoDB 4.4 also gave `$out` cross-database output: "Starting in MongoDB 4.4: `$out` can output to a collection in a different database. In earlier versions, `$out` can only output to a collection in the same database where the aggregation is run." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v4.4/release-notes/4.4.md
34. A `mongodump` started with `--oplog` fails if a client issues an aggregation containing `$out` during the dump. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/

35. MongoDB now positions Atlas Stream Processing as the continuously-maintained counterpart: "On MongoDB Atlas, Atlas Stream Processing can also maintain a streaming materialized view that updates continuously as source data changes." https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/materialized-views/

8. `$out` is atomic from a reader's perspective: it writes to a temp collection, copies the existing collection's index definitions, inserts, then calls `renameCollection` with `dropTarget: true`. "If the aggregation fails, the `$out` operation makes no changes to the pre-existing collection." ([$out reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/out/))

16. `$merge` errors if the operation would change an existing document's `_id` value, or a sharded document's shard key values. Prior writes are still not rolled back. ([$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))

17. If the unique index backing `on` is dropped mid-aggregation, "there is no guarantee that the aggregation will be killed. If the aggregation continues, there is no guarantee that documents do not have duplicate `on` field values." A concurrent index-maintenance job can therefore silently corrupt the view's key uniqueness. ([$merge reference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/merge/))
